identity.name: UNITA

alt_names: National Union for the Total Independence of Angola
Democratic People's Republic of Angola (Huambo government, 1975)

capitals.name: Huambo
capitals.note: Upon independence in 1975 'Savimbi declared Huambo the capital of the Democratic People's Republic of Angola'; 'the MPLA took the city back on 8 February 1976 with the help of Cuban troops.'

capitals.name: Jamba
capitals.note: 'Jamba served as UNITA's headquarters from 1976 until 1992'; Jamba is in the south-eastern province of Cuando Cubango (municipality of Luiana). The UNITA page: 'UNITA later moved to Jamba in Angola's southeastern province of Cuando Cubango'. Coordinates 17.45583 S, 22.61306 E as the page gives them.

capitals.name: Huambo
capitals.note: 'UNITA defensively moved their base from Jamba to Huambo' after fighting began in October 1992; the city was taken on 7 March 1993 and lost to a government offensive on 9 November 1994 (Huambo page).

capitals.name: Bailundo
capitals.note: After the November 1994 offensive 'The UNITA headquarters was then moved to Jamba' and 'UNITA moved again its headquarters soon after signing the protocol, this time to Bailundo', some 50 km north of Huambo; the Bailundo page: 'In the 1990s, Bailundo was the location of the headquarters of UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi.' 'The Government retook the town of Bailundo in October 1999' (Huambo page). The short stay at Jamba in November 1994 is not entered. Coordinates 12.19583 S, 15.85556 E from the Bailundo page. The pages give no seat after October 1999 (Jamba itself 'was captured by Angolan military forces' on 24 December 1999).

correction.text: Huambo, where UNITA 'set up a second government, the Democratic People's Republic of Angola'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (Cliopatria has no row). The FNLA-UNITA coalition government sat at Huambo from late November 1975; the page gives no exact date and no further territory.

correction.text: 'controlled much of the highland's interior, notably the Bie Plateau' (1975-2002), without Huambo, which the MPLA took back on 8 February 1976

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The Bie Plateau is the contested core (contest_start 1975-11), not solid rebel land; Huambo is removed because the loss of 8 February 1976 (ledger) ends the 1975 keyframe. The UNITA page gives no percentages or years of control. UNITA's headquarters stood at Jamba in Cuando Cubango from 1976 to 1992 (Jamba page, a capital of this dossier), but no page opened gives the land it held around Jamba, so none is drawn; the Andulo page opened for 1994-99 says nothing of the war. The region 'Bie plateau' of the gazetteer (Benguela, Huambo, Bie and Cuanza Sul) is wider than the interior the page names.

correction.text: the Bie Plateau with Huambo, taken by UNITA on 7 March 1993 after a 55-day battle and lost on 9 November 1994

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The ledger's 1993-03 gain returns Huambo to UNITA; 'By August 1993, UNITA had gained control over 70% of Angola', which no region can express. The 1994-11 loss ends this keyframe: it holds for 1993 and 1994, the post-loss shape starting in 1995.

correction.text: the Bie Plateau without Huambo: the countryside around the Bailundo headquarters (1994-1999) and the interior until the April 2002 ceasefire

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. After the government retook Huambo on 9 November 1994 UNITA's headquarters moved to Bailundo, 50 km north; 'The Government retook the town of Bailundo in October 1999' and Jamba fell on 24 December 1999 (Jamba page). The pages give no UNITA-held land for 2000-2002 beyond the UNITA page's 'much of the highland's interior' (1975-2002), so the shape is carried to the April 2002 ceasefire as a soft contest zone.

ledger.note: 1975: UNITA sets up a rival government at Huambo. UNITA 'was nearly destroyed in November 1975, but it managed to survive and set up a second government, the Democratic People's Republic of Angola, in the provincial capital of Huambo.' UNITA itself was founded on 13 March 1966 at Muangai, Moxico (same page); the page gives no exact date for the Huambo government.

1975: the fight for the highlands opens. UNITA 'controlled much of the highland's interior, notably the Bie Plateau' during the civil war (1975-2002); the Angolan Civil War page dates the war from independence in November 1975.

region.text: 'the MPLA took the city back on 8 February 1976 with the help of Cuban troops'

ledger.note: 1976: the MPLA takes Huambo back. Huambo page: 'the MPLA took the city back on 8 February 1976 with the help of Cuban troops'; the page says Savimbi had declared Huambo the capital of the Democratic People's Republic of Angola on independence in 1975. The Angola dossier carries the mirror gain (and the 1975-11 loss that matches this dossier's found event).
1993: UNITA takes Huambo. 'UNITA began a 55-day battle over Huambo' and gained control on 7 March 1993; 'By August 1993, UNITA had gained control over 70% of Angola.'

region.text: 'A large offensive gave back to the Government the control of Huambo on 9 November'

ledger.note: 1994: the government retakes Huambo. Huambo page: 'The armed conflict flared up again in August 1994. A large offensive gave back to the Government the control of Huambo on 9 November', and soon after all other provincial capitals; 'The UNITA headquarters was then moved to Jamba' and later to Bailundo. The Angolan Civil War page: 'By November 1994, the government had taken control of 60% of the country.' UNITA keeps the countryside of the province (Bailundo until October 1999); the event is the province-level mirror of the Angola gain.
2002: the war ends. Infobox '11 November 1975 - 4 April 2002'.

region.text: the highland interior UNITA held, without Huambo (back with the government since November 1994)

ledger.note: 2002: UNITA lays down its arms. Six weeks after Savimbi's death (22 February 2002) UNITA 'agreed to a ceasefire with the government'; 'In August 2002 UNITA officially gave up its armed wing' and became a political party.

wars.name: Angolan Civil War
wars.outcome: Government victory after Savimbi's death on 22 February 2002; ceasefire in April 2002.
wars.note: Fighting resumed in Huambo in October 1992 (UNITA page); the Lusaka Protocol was signed on 31 October 1994 (Angolan Civil War page) and the war resumed in 1998.

certainty.note: No page opened draws a line of control; the Bie Plateau and Huambo are the researcher's reading of 'much of the highland's interior'.

notes: Rebel dossier added by af-08-m because UNITA held land for more than a year (1975-2002) and Cliopatria has no row. Not settled: the extent of UNITA-held land by year (the pages give only Huambo, the Bie Plateau, and a 70% figure for August 1993); Jamba (Cuando Cubango) is now a capital for 1976-1992 (Jamba page: 'from 1976 until 1992'; coordinates from that page; the gazetteer lacks the name) but the land UNITA held around it is not given by any page, so none is drawn; Bailundo and Andulo as UNITA strongholds: the Huambo page gives Bailundo as the headquarters from late 1994 and retaken in October 1999 (now a capital), the Andulo page opened says nothing of the war. UNITA was founded on 13 March 1966 against Portuguese rule; the dossier begins when it holds a government and land (November 1975). The FNLA, the other partner of the Huambo government, has no dossier. Repair run of 2026-10-24: the Huambo page adds the loss of Huambo on 8 February 1976 and on 9 November 1994 (the page leaves the year of the second to be inferred from 'flared up again in August 1994'); keyframes now follow the ledger (1975 Huambo; 1976-1992 plateau without Huambo; 1993-1994 plateau with Huambo; 1995-2002 plateau without Huambo). The reviewer's remark that a separate 'Democratic People's Republic of Angola' dossier would double the 1975 Huambo land is accepted: it stays an alt name and the 1975 keyframe here.
